title: Current Affairs — How to Prepare
summary: The static layer of current affairs: how CA questions are framed, the award, sports, summit, day and index categories to track every month, and the pairing-based method to revise them — structure that never expires, whatever the news cycle.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Award categories and structures in the news
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'X award is given in the field of', 'the highest civilian award', 'Dronacharya honours whom', plus statement sets on instituting years and first recipients.
pyqPatterns.approach: Revise ladders, not winners: Bharat Ratna > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri (all 1954); PVC > MVC > Vir (wartime) and Ashoka > Kirti > Shaurya (peacetime); Khel Ratna > Arjuna (players) > Dronacharya (coaches) > Dhyan Chand (lifetime) > MAKA (university). Years: Jnanpith 1965, Phalke 1969, Nobel 1901/Economics 1969, Magsaysay 1957.

example.q: The **Dronacharya Award** is given to —
example.solution: Outstanding **coaches** (instituted 1985) — players receive the Arjuna Award.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Sports event facts: host, motto, mascot and tally
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The X tournament was hosted by', 'which country won', 'the mascot was', or statements mixing host, champion and cycle.
pyqPatterns.approach: One line per event in the window: host — champion — India's highlight — any record. Cycles: four-yearly (Olympics, CWG, Asian Games, FIFA, ODI WC), biennial (T20 WC, Thomas/Uber), annual (IPL, Khelo India). Static pins: Olympics 1896 Athens/IOC Lausanne, Asian Games 1951 New Delhi, Cricket WC 1975.

example.q: The **Thomas Cup** is related to which sport?
example.solution: **Badminton** (men's team) — Uber Cup is the women's counterpart; India first won in 2022.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Summits and groupings: host, theme, membership, HQ
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The latest X summit was held at', 'who chairs/members', 'the headquarters of the grouping is', and India in-or-out statements.
pyqPatterns.approach: Memorise per group: HQ and members first (SCO Beijing, SAARC Kathmandu-8, BIMSTEC Dhaka-7, ASEAN Jakarta, UN New York-193, Commonwealth London-56), then the window's host and theme. India in: G20, BRICS, SCO, QUAD, SAARC, BIMSTEC, Commonwealth. India out: APEC, ASEAN, G7, NATO, OPEC.

example.q: The **African Union** became a permanent G20 member at which summit?
example.solution: The **New Delhi G20 (2023)** — the second regional bloc after the EU.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'X day is observed to commemorate', 'whose birth anniversary', matching columns of days, months and causes.
pyqPatterns.approach: Person-days: Vivekananda 12 Jan, B.C. Roy 1 Jul, Dhyan Chand 29 Aug, Radhakrishnan 5 Sep, Patel 31 Oct, Nehru 14 Nov, Ramanujan 22 Dec. Event-days: Raman effect 28 Feb, Pokhran 11 May 1998, Trident 4 Dec, Constitution adoption 26 Nov (since 2015). UN set: Yoga 21 Jun (India's proposal, first 2015), Environment 5 Jun, HR 10 Dec.

example.q: **National Science Day** (28 February) commemorates —
example.solution: The discovery of the **Raman effect** (1928).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which organisation releases the X index', match-the-column of indexes and publishers, and 'which pairing is wrong' options.
pyqPatterns.approach: Grid by publisher family: UNDP (HDI), UN SDSN (Happiness, global SDG), WIPO (Innovation), IMF (WEO), World Bank (Human Capital; Doing Business discontinued 2021 → B-READY), WEF (Gender Gap, Risks, Tourism), Transparency International (corruption CPI), IEP (Peace), RSF (Press Freedom), Concern + Welthungerhilfe (Hunger — the NGO trap), IMD, EIU, Yale/Columbia (EPI). India: NITI (SDG India, Innovation), RBI (FI-Index), Pratham (ASER).

example.q: The **Global Hunger Index** is released by —
example.solution: **Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe** — two NGOs; naming a UN body is the planted error.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who has been appointed as', match-the-column of posts and persons, and 'which office does X hold' one-liners from the window.
pyqPatterns.approach: For every appointment note **person ↔ post** in one line, and the appointment layer beneath it: President appoints Governors, CJI, CEC, CAG; collegium route for judges; regulators by the government under their Acts. Posts change — revise the window's list twice before the exam; the appointment mechanism itself is static and permanent.

example.q: A Governor of a state is appointed by —
example.solution: The **President** of India (Article 155) — the static layer under every gubernatorial appointment news item.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two or three numbered statements blend one wrong detail — a wrong host city, ministry, year or publisher — into otherwise correct news facts.
pyqPatterns.approach: Attack the most checkable statement first: years, publishers and HQs rarely change, so a wrong one is quickly provable. 'APEC member', 'WPI target', 'Padma Shri highest', 'SAARC at Dhaka' are recurring planted errors. One verified falsehood eliminates every option containing that statement.

example.q: Consider: 1. NITI Aayog releases the SDG India Index. 2. The Global Hunger Index is a UNDP product. Which are correct?
example.solution: Statement 1 only — the Hunger Index belongs to **Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe**, not UNDP.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A news item (award, summit, launch, day) is cited and the question pivots to its permanent structure — founding year, article, ministry, organising body.
pyqPatterns.approach: Keep a bridge list per bucket: award news → instituting year and first recipient; summit news → group founding and HQ; scheme news → ministry and launch year; day news → the person or event commemorated; index news → publisher. The static layer is the durable half of the question — learn it once, reuse every cycle.

example.q: A news item reports the newest **Human Development Report**. The permanent fact to recall is —
example.solution: The **HDI is published by the UNDP** — publisher pairings outlive every edition.

subtopics.title: How current-affairs questions are framed
subtopics.concept: CA questions come in four frames — **direct recall**, **match-the-column**, **statement-based** and the **CA-to-static bridge**. Track ten buckets monthly: appointments, awards, sports, summits, schemes, defence, space, indexes, days, economy. Note the **pairing** (person↔post, award↔field, day↔theme, index↔publisher), work from a 6-12 month window, and revise one monthly source three times.

tricks.title: Pairing drill
tricks.body: Read any news item and write its two halves — e.g. 'X award → field', 'Y summit → host'. Exams ask the halves, not the story.

example.q: A new Chief Justice is sworn in. What do you note?
example.solution: Post ↔ person (and the appointment mechanism — collegium recommendation, President's appointment) — not the ceremony details.

mistakes: Reading five sources once each instead of one source revised thrice.
Studying the news story while ignoring the pairing the exam actually asks.
Assuming CA never connects back to static GK.
subtopics.notes:
### How current-affairs questions are actually framed
CA questions rarely ask for a whole news story — they convert one news fact into one of four frames:
1. **Direct recall** — 'X won the Y award', 'who holds office Z', 'the summit was hosted by' — one fact, four options.
2. **Match-the-column** — pairs like award ↔ field, day ↔ theme, summit ↔ host, index ↔ publisher; one wrong letter kills the option.
3. **Statement-based** — 2-3 numbered statements mix one wrong detail (wrong year, wrong ministry, wrong city) into two correct ones.
4. **CA-to-static bridge** — news as a doorway to permanent facts: a Nobel announcement revisits Nobel's categories; a summit revisits the group's membership and HQ; a new scheme revisits its ministry.

### The ten recurring buckets to track every month
1. **Appointments and offices** (President, Governors, CJI, chiefs, regulators, international heads).
2. **Awards and honours** (national: Bharat Ratna, Padma, gallantry; international: Nobel, Magsaysay, Booker).
3. **Sports** — winners, hosts, tournaments, records.
4. **Summits and conferences** — host country, theme, outcomes.
5. **Schemes and launches** — new schemes, portal/mission launches, extensions.
6. **Defence exercises and deals** — exercise names (India ↔ partner), missiles, induction.
7. **Space missions** — ISRO launches, landings, satellites.
8. **Indexes and reports** — India's rank and the publisher.
9. **Important days and themes** — especially UN days and their annual themes.
10. **Economy news** — RBI policy reviews, budgets, GST council decisions, big reports.

### The working method
- **Window**: most exams draw from roughly the **previous 6-12 months** before the exam date; monthly compilations cover this systematically.
- **One source, revised thrice**: a monthly compilation read once, revised after a month, and again in the last week beats five half-read sources.
- **Note the pairing, not the story**: for every item, note (person ↔ post), (award ↔ field), (event ↔ host), (day ↔ theme), (index ↔ publisher) — exams ask the pairing.
- **Static-first reading**: attach news to its static root (a grouping's founding year, an award's instituting year) — that part never expires.
- **Skip the noise**: opinion pieces, ongoing court arguments and speculation are rarely asked; anniversaries, firsts and superlatives (largest, first, fastest) are asked constantly.

### Quick revision
- Four frames: direct recall, match-the-column, statement-based, CA-to-static bridge.
- Ten buckets: appointments, awards, sports, summits, schemes, defence, space, indexes, days, economy.
- Working window ≈ previous 6-12 months; monthly compilation + three revisions.
- Exams test the **pairing** (person↔post, award↔field, day↔theme, index↔publisher).
- Attach every news item to its static root; anniversaries, firsts and superlatives score most.

patterns.name: Identify the question frame
patterns.howToSpot: The question itself describes how a news item was asked — 'which frame converts an award announcement into match-the-column' — or asks which preparation method suits a frame.
patterns.logic:
1. Four frames: direct recall (single fact), match-the-column (pairs), statement-based (one wrong detail hidden in correct ones), CA-to-static bridge (news → permanent fact).
2. Statement-based questions are cracked by eliminating the one planted error — a wrong year, ministry or city.
3. Match-the-column is cracked by verifying each pair independently.

example.q: A question gives **three numbered statements about a summit** and asks which are correct. The frame is —
example.solution: **Statement-based** — typically two true statements carry one planted error (wrong host city, wrong year or wrong membership), so test each statement against its static root.

patterns.name: The ten tracking buckets
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which of the following is NOT usually asked from current affairs', categories of news to track monthly, what a monthly compilation covers.
patterns.logic:
1. The ten buckets: appointments, awards, sports, summits, schemes, defence exercises, space, indexes, important days, economy.
2. Rarely asked: opinion columns, speculation, ongoing legal argument, celebrity gossip.
3. Most asked within buckets: **firsts, superlatives, anniversaries and India-specific items**.

example.q: Which type of news is **least likely** to appear as an exam question?
example.solution: **Opinion pieces and speculation** — exams ask settled facts: appointments, award winners, summit hosts, index ranks and launches, never editorial views.

patterns.name: Window and revision method
patterns.howToSpot: Questions on how far back a compilation should reach, how many revisions to plan, or what the 6-month convention is.
patterns.logic:
1. Standard window: the **previous 6-12 months** before the exam (longer for Banking mains).
2. Method: one monthly source, revised **three times** (same month, after a month, exam week).
3. Note **pairings**, not stories — every revision is a pairing drill.

example.q: The usual **preparation window** for current affairs in a typical exam is —
example.solution: About the **previous 6-12 months** before the exam — covered through monthly compilations and revised multiple times.

patterns.name: CA-to-static bridging
patterns.howToSpot: 'A Nobel announcement helps revise which static topic', questions showing a news item and asking the permanent fact it connects to.
patterns.logic:
1. Every news category has a static root: awards → award structure and instituting years; summits → group membership and HQ; schemes → ministry and launch year; days → person or event commemorated.
2. Learn the static root once — it serves every future news cycle.
3. In the exam, the static root often IS the answer even when the question names a recent event.

example.q: A news item says a new **Global Innovation Index** edition is out. The permanent fact it anchors is —
example.solution: The **Global Innovation Index is published by WIPO** (World Intellectual Property Organization) — the index ↔ publisher pairing never changes with the year's edition.

subtopics.title: Award categories to track — structure, not winners
subtopics.concept: Learn the ladders, not the winners: civilian **Bharat Ratna (1954) > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri**; gallantry wartime **PVC > MVC > Vir Chakra**, peacetime **Ashoka > Kirti > Shaurya Chakra**; sports **Khel Ratna (1991-92, renamed 2021) > Arjuna (1961) > Dronacharya (1985, coaches)**; literature **Jnanpith (1965)**, cinema **Dadasaheb Phalke (1969)**; global **Nobel (1901, Economics 1969, Peace at Oslo)** and **Magsaysay (1957, Manila)**.

tricks.title: Ladder memory
tricks.body: Civilian: **Ratna > Vibhushan > Bhushan > Shri**. Sports: **Khel Ratna > Arjuna (players) > Dronacharya (coaches)** — teachers below students is the joke that fixes the order.

example.q: Fourth-highest civilian honour?
example.solution: Padma Shri — count down the ladder; 'Shri' rhymes with 'fourth' is a common mnemonic.

mistakes: Calling Param Vir Chakra a civilian award — it is the highest *wartime gallantry* medal.
Placing Padma Shri above Padma Bhushan.
subtopics.notes:
### Civilian awards — the ladder
| Award | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **Bharat Ratna** | Highest civilian honour; instituted **1954**; first: **C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan, C.V. Raman** (1954); first woman: **Indira Gandhi** (1971); first posthumous: **Lal Bahadur Shastri** (1966); first sportsperson: **Sachin Tendulkar** (2014) |
| **Padma Vibhushan** | Second-highest civilian award |
| **Padma Bhushan** | Third-highest |
| **Padma Shri** | Fourth-highest; all Padma awards instituted **1954**, announced on **Republic Day eve** |

### Gallantry awards — two ladders
- **Wartime**: **Param Vir Chakra** (highest, instituted 26 January 1950) → **Maha Vir Chakra** → **Vir Chakra**.
- **Peacetime**: **Ashoka Chakra** (highest peacetime) → **Kirti Chakra** → **Shaurya Chakra**. Gallantry awards are announced around **Republic Day and Independence Day**.

### Literary, film and global prizes
- **Jnanpith Award** — highest literary honour; first given **1965** to **G. Sankara Kurup** (Malayalam).
- **Sahitya Akademi Award** — given by the National Akademi of Letters (est. 1954).
- **Dadasaheb Phalke Award** — highest cinema honour; instituted **1969**; first recipient **Devika Rani**.
- **Nobel Prizes** — from **Alfred Nobel's will (1895)**, first awarded **1901**; six categories: Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, Peace, and the **Economics prize added in 1969** (Sveriges Riksbank prize). All are awarded in **Stockholm** except **Peace, awarded in Oslo**.
- **Ramon Magsaysay Award** — the 'Asian Nobel', instituted **1957**, presented at **Manila**.
- **Booker Prize** — leading English-fiction prize; **International Booker** honours translated works.

### Sports awards — the pyramid
| Award | Field | Instituted |
|---|---|---|
| **Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna** | Highest sporting honour (named **renamed in 2021** from Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna, instituted 1991-92) | 1991-92 |
| **Arjuna Award** | Consistent outstanding performance | 1961 |
| **Dronacharya Award** | **Coaches** | 1985 |
| **Major Dhyan Chand Award** (lifetime achievement) | Contribution to sports | 2002 |
| **MAKA Trophy** | Best **university** | 1956-57 |

### Reading an award question
Exams test three layers, all permanent: the **ladder** (which is highest), the **instituting year / first recipient**, and **award ↔ field** matching (Dronacharya = coaches, MAKA = university). The winner of the current cycle changes; the structure never does — revise the structure once and every year's news plugs in.

### Quick revision
- Civilian ladder: Bharat Ratna (1954) > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri; announced Republic Day eve.
- Bharat Ratna firsts: 1954 trio; woman — Indira Gandhi; posthumous — Shastri; sportsperson — Tendulkar.
- Gallantry: wartime PVC-MVC-Vir; peacetime Ashoka-Kirti-Shaurya.
- Jnanpith 1965 (Sankara Kurup); Dadasaheb Phalke 1969 (Devika Rani); Nobel 1901, Economics 1969, Peace in Oslo.
- Magsaysay 1957 Manila; Booker for English fiction.
- Sports: Khel Ratna 1991-92 (renamed 2021), Arjuna 1961, Dronacharya 1985 (coaches), Dhyan Chand 2002 (lifetime), MAKA (university).

patterns.name: Civilian awards: ladder and firsts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is the highest civilian award', 'the first woman to receive Bharat Ratna', ordering of Padma awards, first posthumous or sportsperson facts.
patterns.logic:
1. Ladder: **Bharat Ratna > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri**; all instituted **1954**, announced **Republic Day eve**.
2. Bharat Ratna firsts: 1954 trio (Rajagopalachari, Radhakrishnan, Raman); woman — **Indira Gandhi 1971**; posthumous — **Shastri 1966**; sportsperson — **Tendulkar 2014**.
3. 'Fourth-highest civilian honour' = **Padma Shri** — a frequent answer.

example.q: The **first posthumous Bharat Ratna** was awarded to —
example.solution: **Lal Bahadur Shastri** (1966) — honoured the year after his death at Tashkent; the award's first woman recipient was Indira Gandhi (1971).

patterns.name: Sports awards: award ↔ field matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Dronacharya Award is given to', 'the highest sports honour is', 'MAKA Trophy relates to', matching each sports award with its field.
patterns.logic:
1. **Khel Ratna** = highest sporting honour (renamed Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna in **2021**; instituted 1991-92).
2. **Dronacharya = coaches** (1985); **Arjuna = players** (1961); **Dhyan Chand Award = lifetime contribution** (2002); **MAKA = best university**.
3. Year anchors kill wrong options instantly.

example.q: The **Dronacharya Award** honours —
example.solution: Outstanding **coaches** — instituted 1985; players receive the Arjuna Award instead.

patterns.name: Nobel prize structure
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded at', 'which category was added in 1969', 'the Nobel prizes are given from whose bequest'.
patterns.logic:
1. Origin: **Alfred Nobel's will (1895)**; first awarded **1901**; five original categories.
2. **Economics (1969)** is the later 'Sveriges Riksbank' prize — the classic 'which is NOT an original Nobel' answer.
3. Venue: **Oslo for Peace**, **Stockholm for the rest**.

example.q: The Nobel Prize in **Economics** differs from the original prizes because —
example.solution: It was **added in 1969** (the Sveriges Riksbank Prize) — the original five came from Alfred Nobel's 1895 will, first given in 1901.

patterns.name: Gallantry awards: wartime vs peacetime
patterns.howToSpot: 'The highest wartime gallantry award', 'Ashoka Chakra is given for', ordering questions on Chakra series.
patterns.logic:
1. Wartime ladder: **Param Vir Chakra > Maha Vir Chakra > Vir Chakra** (PVC instituted 26 January 1950).
2. Peacetime ladder: **Ashoka Chakra > Kirti Chakra > Shaurya Chakra**.
3. Never mix the ladders — 'highest gallantry award' without a qualifier means **PVC (wartime)**.

example.q: India's **highest peacetime gallantry award** is —
example.solution: The **Ashoka Chakra** — wartime equivalent is the Param Vir Chakra (1950); Kirti Chakra and Shaurya Chakra follow it.

patterns.name: Literature, film and international prizes
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Jnanpith Award was first won by', 'Dadasaheb Phalke Award relates to', 'the Asian Nobel is', matching prizes with fields and first recipients.
patterns.logic:
1. **Jnanpith** — highest literary award, first **1965**, **G. Sankara Kurup**; **Sahitya Akademi** — the Akademi's own award.
2. **Dadasaheb Phalke (1969, Devika Rani)** — highest cinema honour; **Booker** — English fiction; **International Booker** — translation.
3. **Magsaysay (1957, Manila)** — the 'Asian Nobel'; **Oscars/Academy Awards** — since 1929.

example.q: The **Ramon Magsaysay Award**, often called the 'Asian Nobel', is presented in —
example.solution: **Manila, Philippines** — instituted in **1957** for public service and leadership across Asia.

subtopics.concept: For every tournament note five: **host, motto/theme, mascot, champion, India's highlight**. Cycles: Olympics/CWG/Asian Games/FIFA/ODI WC four-yearly; T20 WC and Thomas/Uber biennial; IPL and Khelo India annual. Firsts: Olympics 1896 Athens, Winter 1924, CWG 1930, Asian Games 1951 New Delhi, Cricket WC 1975. India: 1900 debut, 8 hockey golds, Bindra 2008, Thomas Cup 2022.

tricks.title: Cycle split
tricks.body: Four-yearly: Olympics, Winter, CWG, Asian Games, FIFA, ODI WC. **Two-yearly: T20 WC, Thomas/Uber**. Annual: IPL, Ranji, Khelo India.

example.q: How often is the T20 World Cup held?
example.solution: Every two years — the ODI World Cup is the four-yearly one.

mistakes: Mixing the two-year T20 World Cup cycle with the four-yearly ODI World Cup.
Swapping Thomas Cup (badminton) into football or tennis options.
Attributing the first Asian Games to Bangkok instead of New Delhi (1951).
subtopics.notes:
### How sports CA is asked
Every tournament question recycles the same five details: **host country/city, motto or theme, mascot, the champion (and runner-up), and India's performance** (medal tally, records, firsts). Note those five for every event in your window; learn the **cycle and organiser** of each event permanently.

### The recurring events and their cycles
| Event | Cycle | Structural facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Olympics (Summer)** | 4 years | Modern Games from **1896 Athens**, revived by **Pierre de Coubertin**; **IOC** (1894) at **Lausanne**; motto 'Citius, Altius, **Communius**' (together, added 2021); five rings |
| **Winter Olympics** | 4 years, offset | First: **1924 Chamonix** |
| **Paralympics** | with Olympics | For athletes with disabilities |
| **Commonwealth Games** | 4 years | Began as **British Empire Games, 1930 Hamilton** |
| **Asian Games** | 4 years | First: **1951 New Delhi**; run by the **OCA** |
| **FIFA World Cup** | 4 years | First: **1930 Uruguay** |
| **ICC Cricket World Cup (ODI)** | 4 years | First: **1975 England**; India won **1983, 2011** |
| **ICC T20 World Cup** | 2 years | India won the first, **2007** |
| **IPL** | annual | BCCI's T20 league, from **2008** |
| **Ranji Trophy** | annual | Indian first-class championship (1934), named after **Ranjitsinhji** |
| **Khelo India Games** | annual | From **2018**, school + university tiers |
| **Thomas Cup / Uber Cup** | 2 years | Men's / women's **badminton** team events |

### India anchors — permanent facts
- First Olympics participation: **1900 Paris** (**Norman Pritchard**, two athletics silvers).
- **Hockey: eight Olympic golds** — the run began at **1928 Amsterdam**; last gold **1980 Moscow**.
- First **individual** Olympic gold: **Abhinav Bindra** (2008, 10 m air rifle); **Neeraj Chopra** took javelin gold at the Tokyo Games.
- First Cricket World Cup win: **1983** under Kapil Dev at Lord's; T20 in **2007**; 2011 under M.S. Dhoni.
- India won the **Thomas Cup** for the first time in **2022** — a settled historical fact now.

### How to note a tournament
For each event in the window, record one line: *event — year — host — champion — India's highlight — any record*. Statements in exams typically swap **one** of these (a wrong host city or a wrong champion); the rest stay true. Superlatives recur too: oldest tournament (Durand Cup, 1888, Asia's oldest football cup), oldest tennis event (Wimbledon, 1877), the Davis Cup in men's tennis.

### Quick revision
- Note five: host, motto/theme, mascot, champion, India's highlight.
- Olympics 1896 Athens (Coubertin); IOC Lausanne; Winter 1924 Chamonix; CWG from 1930 Hamilton.
- Asian Games first at **New Delhi (1951)**; FIFA WC 1930; Cricket WC 1975 (India: 1983, 2011); T20 biennial.
- IPL 2008; Ranji 1934; Khelo India 2018; Thomas/Uber = badminton team cups.
- India: 1900 first participation; hockey 8 golds; Bindra first individual gold (2008); Thomas Cup 2022.

patterns.name: Tournament ↔ sport / organiser matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Thomas Cup is related to which sport', 'the Ranji Trophy is associated with', 'which body conducts the IPL', matching events with sports.
patterns.logic:
1. Cup ↔ sport pins: **Thomas (men) / Uber (women)** = badminton; **Davis** = tennis; **Santosh** = football (states); **Ranji** = cricket (first-class); **Durand** = football (Asia's oldest, 1888).
2. **IPL** = BCCI (from 2008); **Khelo India** = government's annual games (2018).
3. The odd option in such questions is usually a swapped sport.

example.q: The **Thomas Cup** is associated with —
example.solution: **Men's badminton** (team event) — its women's counterpart is the **Uber Cup**; India first won the Thomas Cup in 2022.

patterns.name: Cycles and first editions
patterns.howToSpot: 'How often is the T20 World Cup held', 'the first Asian Games were held at', 'the first Cricket World Cup was played in', year and cycle questions.
patterns.logic:
1. 4-yearly: Olympics, Winter Olympics (offset), CWG, Asian Games, FIFA WC, ODI Cricket WC. **Biennial**: T20 WC, Thomas/Uber Cups.
2. First editions: Olympics **1896 Athens**; Winter **1924**; CWG **1930**; Asian Games **1951 New Delhi**; FIFA **1930**; ODI WC **1975**.
3. Annual: IPL (2008), Ranji (1934), Khelo India (2018).

example.q: The **first Asian Games** were hosted by —
example.solution: **New Delhi (1951)** — a home-soil first that exams return to; the Games are held every four years under the OCA.

patterns.name: Olympic facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'The modern Olympics began in', 'the IOC is headquartered at', 'the Olympic motto is', questions on rings, motto, founder.
patterns.logic:
1. Modern Games: **1896 Athens**, revived by **Pierre de Coubertin**; **IOC (1894)** sits at **Lausanne**.
2. Motto: 'Citius, Altius, **Communius**' (Faster, Higher, Stronger-*Together* — 'Communius' added 2021); **five interlocking rings**.
3. Winter Games separate, first **1924 Chamonix**; Paralympics follow the main Games.

example.q: The headquarters of the **International Olympic Committee** is at —
example.solution: **Lausanne, Switzerland** — the IOC, founded in 1894, revived the Games at Athens in 1896.

patterns.name: India-specific sports records
patterns.howToSpot: 'India's first individual Olympic gold', 'how many hockey golds', 'India first won the Thomas Cup in', permanent India anchors.
patterns.logic:
1. **1900 Paris** = first participation (Norman Pritchard); **hockey = 8 Olympic golds** (1928-1980 era).
2. **Abhinav Bindra (2008)** = first individual gold; **Neeraj Chopra** = javelin gold (Tokyo Games).
3. Cricket: 1983 (ODI), 2007 (T20), 2011; **Thomas Cup 2022** first win.

example.q: India's first **individual Olympic gold medal** was won by —
example.solution: **Abhinav Bindra** — 10 m air rifle at the **2008 Beijing** Games; the hockey team had won team golds since 1928.

patterns.name: Champion-host-mascot statement sets
patterns.howToSpot: Statements mixing one wrong host city, champion or mascot into correct sports facts; ordering of tournaments by year.
patterns.logic:
1. For every event in the window, memorise the line: event — host — champion — India's highlight.
2. In statements, the wrong detail is usually the **host city** or **champion**; years and sports are less often swapped.
3. Superlatives recur: Durand (1888) oldest in Asia; Wimbledon (1877) oldest in tennis.

example.q: Consider: 1. The IPL is conducted by the BCCI. 2. The Durand Cup is a hockey tournament. 3. Wimbledon is the oldest tennis championship. Which are correct?
example.solution: Statements 1 and 3 only — the **Durand Cup is football** (Asia's oldest, since 1888); IPL-BCCI and Wimbledon's seniority are correct.

subtopics.title: Summits, groupings and organisations to track
subtopics.concept: Note **host city, theme, membership change, HQ** per summit. Anchors: UN 1945 (193 members, UNSC 5+10), NAM 1961, ASEAN 1967 Jakarta, SAARC 1985 Kathmandu (8), BIMSTEC 1997 Dhaka (7), G20 1999/2008 (AU joined 2023), SCO 2001 Beijing (India-Pak 2017), first BRICS summit 2009 (NDB Shanghai), Commonwealth 56/London. India is **not** in APEC, ASEAN, G7, NATO or OPEC.

tricks.title: HQ trio
tricks.body: **SCO — Beijing; SAARC — Kathmandu; BIMSTEC — Dhaka** — the three most-swapped headquarters. ASEAN sits at Jakarta as the fourth.

example.q: BIMSTEC's secretariat is at?
example.solution: Dhaka — while SAARC (the other South Asian bloc) is at Kathmandu.

mistakes: Marking India an APEC member — it is not.
Putting SAARC's HQ at Dhaka (that is BIMSTEC); SAARC sits at Kathmandu.
Confusing the G20's founding (1999) with its first leaders' summit (2008).
subtopics.notes:
### What summit questions ask
Four details, every time: **host country/city of the latest summit, the group's membership, its headquarters, and what changed** (a new member, a theme, an outcome). The membership and HQ are permanent; learn them once.

### The groupings to know cold
| Grouping | Founded | HQ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G20** | 1999 (finance ministers); leaders' summits from 2008 | No permanent HQ — rotating presidency | 19 countries + the **European Union**; the **African Union joined in 2023** (New Delhi summit) |
| **BRICS** | term coined 2001; first summit **2009** | NDB at Shanghai | Brazil, Russia, India, China, **South Africa (2010)**; expansion approved **2024** (Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE among entrants) |
| **SCO** | **2001** (from the Shanghai Five) | **Beijing** (RATS at Tashkent) | India and Pakistan full members since **2017**; Belarus joined **2024** |
| **QUAD** | 2007, revived **2017** | — (no HQ) | India, USA, Japan, Australia; leaders'-level since 2021 |
| **ASEAN** | **1967**, Bangkok Declaration | **Jakarta** | Southeast Asia's ten-nation bloc; India is a dialogue partner, not a member |
| **UN** | **1945** | New York | 51 founders; **193 members**; UNSC = **5 permanent (veto) + 10 non-permanent** (2-year terms) |
| **SAARC** | **1985** (first summit Dhaka) | **Kathmandu** | 8 South Asian members; SAFTA from 2006 |
| **BIMSTEC** | **1997** | **Dhaka** | 7 Bay of Bengal littorals: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand |
| **Commonwealth** | London Declaration 1949 (modern form) | **London** (Marlborough House) | **56 member states**; the British Sovereign is its Head |
| **NAM** | **1961 Belgrade** | — | India a founding member |

### India's membership map — a favourite trap set
**Member**: UN, G20, BRICS, SCO, QUAD, SAARC, BIMSTEC, Commonwealth, NAM, IMF/World Bank/WTO, AIIB, ADB.
**Not a member**: **APEC** (the classic trap), ASEAN (dialogue partner only), G7, NATO, OPEC. India led the **G77** (developing-countries caucus at the UN) at times and hosts the **International Solar Alliance** (HQ Gurugram) with France.

### How to note a summit in the window
One line per event: *group — host city/country — theme — what changed*. Themes are quoted in one-liners; membership changes (AU into G20, Belarus into SCO, BRICS expansion) are the second-most asked detail after hosts.

### Quick revision
- G20: 1999/2008; AU joined 2023; rotating presidency, no HQ.
- BRICS: 2009 first summit; NDB Shanghai; 2024 expansion. SCO: 2001, Beijing; India-Pak 2017.
- QUAD = India-US-Japan-Australia (revived 2017). ASEAN 1967 Jakarta; India = dialogue partner.
- UN 1945, 193 members; UNSC 5+10. SAARC 1985 Kathmandu (8). BIMSTEC 1997 Dhaka (7).
- Commonwealth 56, London. NAM 1961 Belgrade.
- India is NOT in APEC, ASEAN, G7, NATO, OPEC.

patterns.name: Summit ↔ host ↔ theme
patterns.howToSpot: 'The X summit was hosted by', statements pairing a recent summit with its host city or theme.
patterns.logic:
1. For each summit in the window, memorise **group — host city/country — theme** as one line.
2. Themes quoted in exams are usually slogans (e.g. G20 New Delhi's 'One Earth One Family One Future').
3. When options swap cities, eliminate by continent logic first — the wrong pair is almost always from a different region.

example.q: The **G20 summit hosted by India** (New Delhi, 2023) carried the theme —
example.solution: '**Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — One Earth, One Family, One Future**'; the same summit admitted the **African Union** as a permanent member.

patterns.name: Group ↔ membership ↔ headquarters
patterns.howToSpot: 'The SCO is headquartered at', 'how many members does BIMSTEC have', matching groups with HQ and member counts.
patterns.logic:
1. HQ pins: SCO — **Beijing**; SAARC — **Kathmandu**; BIMSTEC — **Dhaka**; ASEAN — **Jakarta**; NDB (BRICS) — **Shanghai**; Commonwealth — **London**.
2. Counts: SAARC **8**; BIMSTEC **7**; UN **193**; Commonwealth **56**; UNSC **5 permanent + 10 non-permanent**.
3. India-led or India-hosted bodies: International Solar Alliance — **Gurugram**.

example.q: The headquarters of the **Shanghai Cooperation Organisation** is at —
example.solution: **Beijing** — the anti-terror arm (RATS) sits at Tashkent; India and Pakistan became full members in 2017.

patterns.name: India's membership map (in / out)
patterns.howToSpot: 'India is NOT a member of', statements placing India inside or outside a grouping — APEC and ASEAN are the classic traps.
patterns.logic:
1. **In**: UN, G20, BRICS, SCO, QUAD, SAARC, BIMSTEC, Commonwealth, NAM, AIIB, ADB.
2. **Out**: **APEC** (the evergreen trap), **ASEAN** (dialogue partner only), G7, NATO, OPEC.
3. Founding credits: India co-founded **NAM, G77 work, SAARC-era bodies and the International Solar Alliance** (with France).

example.q: India is **not** a member of which grouping?
example.solution: **APEC** (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) — despite bordering the Pacific's trade flows, India sits outside it; ASEAN membership is also absent (dialogue partner only).

patterns.name: Groupings: founding years and expansions
patterns.howToSpot: 'BRICS expansion happened in', 'when did India join the SCO', ordering groups by founding year, new-member questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Years: UN 1945, NAM 1961, ASEAN 1967, SAARC 1985, G20 1999, SCO 2001, BIMSTEC 1997, first BRICS summit 2009.
2. Expansions: AU into G20 (**2023**); BRICS expansion (**2024**); Belarus into SCO (**2024**); India-Pakistan into SCO (**2017**).
3. Match the change to the group before checking other statements.

example.q: India and Pakistan became **full members of the SCO** in —
example.solution: **2017** — the SCO (founded 2001) admitted both together; Belarus followed as a full member in 2024.

patterns.name: UN structure and India's UN track
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many members does the UN have', 'UNSC non-permanent members serve for', how many times India has been an elected UNSC member.
patterns.logic:
1. UN: founded **1945**, **193 members**, HQ New York; principal judicial organ **ICJ at The Hague**.
2. **UNSC**: 15 members — 5 permanent with veto (US, UK, France, Russia, China) + 10 non-permanent for **two-year** terms.
3. India has been elected a **non-permanent UNSC member eight times** (latest term 2021-22) and has long pressed for permanent reform.

example.q: Non-permanent members of the **UN Security Council** are elected for a term of —
example.solution: **Two years** — ten of the Council's fifteen seats rotate; the five permanent members hold vetoes.

subtopics.title: Important days — national and UN framework
subtopics.concept: National person-days: Youth 12 Jan (Vivekananda), Sports 29 Aug (Dhyan Chand), Teachers 5 Sep (Radhakrishnan), Unity 31 Oct (Patel), Children 14 Nov (Nehru), Maths 22 Dec (Ramanujan). Event-days: Science 28 Feb (Raman effect), Technology 11 May (Pokhran 1998), Constitution 26 Nov (adopted 1949, observed since 2015). Defence: Army 15 Jan, Air Force 8 Oct, Navy 4 Dec. UN set: Yoga 21 Jun (India's proposal, first 2015), Environment 5 Jun, Human Rights 10 Dec.

tricks.title: Person-day strings
tricks.body: Chain them by date: **12 Jan Vivekananda → 1 Jul B.C. Roy → 29 Aug Dhyan Chand → 5 Sep Radhakrishnan → 31 Oct Patel → 14 Nov Nehru → 22 Dec Ramanujan**.

example.q: National Sports Day honours whom?
example.solution: Major Dhyan Chand — 29 August; the sports awards are conferred the same day.

mistakes: Equating Constitution Day (26 Nov, adoption 1949) with Republic Day (26 Jan, in force 1950).
Confusing Teachers' Day (Radhakrishnan, 5 Sep) with National Education Day (Azad, 11 Nov).
Placing Air Force Day on 4 December — that is Navy Day; the IAF day is 8 October.
subtopics.notes:
### The day ↔ purpose ↔ person framework
Important-day questions come in two stable shapes: **day ↔ what it commemorates** (person, event, charter) and **day ↔ theme of the year** (the theme changes annually — quote only if asked in-window; the day itself never changes). National days usually commemorate a person's birth or a national event; UN days mark charters, conventions and global causes.

### National days — the permanent dozen
| Day | Commemorates |
|---|---|
| **12 January** — National Youth Day | Birth of **Swami Vivekananda** |
| **15 January** — Army Day | **K.M. Cariappa** became first Indian Commander-in-Chief (1949) |
| **28 February** — National Science Day | **Raman effect** discovery (1928) |
| **11 May** — National Technology Day | **Pokhran tests** (11 May 1998) |
| **1 July** — National Doctors' Day | Dr. **B.C. Roy** (birth & death) |
| **29 August** — National Sports Day | **Major Dhyan Chand** |
| **5 September** — Teachers' Day | Dr. **S. Radhakrishnan** |
| **14 September** — Hindi Diwas | Hindi adopted as official language (1949) |
| **31 October** — National Unity Day | Birth of **Sardar Patel** |
| **14 November** — Children's Day | Birth of **Jawaharlal Nehru** |
| **26 November** — Constitution Day | Constitution adopted (1949); observed since **2015** |
| **4 December** — Navy Day | **Operation Trident** (1971) |
| **22 December** — National Mathematics Day | **Srinivasa Ramanujan**; since **2012** |
| **25 December** — Good Governance Day | Birth of **Atal Bihari Vajpayee** |

Defence triple: Army 15 Jan, Air Force **8 October**, Navy 4 December.

### UN international days — the high-frequency set
- **8 March** Women's Day; **22 March** World Water Day; **7 April** World Health Day (WHO founded 1948); **22 April** Earth Day; **3 May** World Press Freedom Day; **5 June** World Environment Day (from the 1972 Stockholm Conference); **21 June** **International Day of Yoga** (UN-declared in 2014 on India's proposal, first observed 2015); **29 July** International Tiger Day; **8 September** International Literacy Day; **2 October** International Day of Non-Violence (Gandhi's birthday); **24 October** UN Day; **10 December** Human Rights Day (UDHR adopted 1948).

### The working method
1. Memorise the **person or event** behind each national day — the exam asks 'National Sports Day marks whose birth anniversary', never the date alone.
2. For UN days, learn the **cause and the Indian connection** (Yoga proposed by India; Environment Day born of Stockholm 1972).
3. Note each year's **theme** for days inside the exam window — themes appear as fill-in-the-blank one-liners.
4. Anniversaries (e.g. '75 years of the Constitution') ride on these same dates — the static date is the anchor.

### Quick revision
- Person-days: Youth 12 Jan (Vivekananda), Sports 29 Aug (Dhyan Chand), Teachers 5 Sep (Radhakrishnan), Unity 31 Oct (Patel), Children 14 Nov (Nehru), Maths 22 Dec (Ramanujan).
- Event-days: Science 28 Feb (Raman effect), Technology 11 May (Pokhran 1998), Navy 4 Dec (Trident), Constitution 26 Nov (adopted 1949).
- Defence: Army 15 Jan, Air Force 8 Oct, Navy 4 Dec.
- UN set: Yoga 21 Jun (India's proposal), Environment 5 Jun, Health 7 Apr, HR 10 Dec, Non-Violence 2 Oct, UN Day 24 Oct.

patterns.name: Day ↔ person commemorated
patterns.howToSpot: 'National Sports Day marks whose birth anniversary', 'Teachers' Day commemorates', matching person-days with names.
patterns.logic:
1. Person-days: Vivekananda 12 Jan; B.C. Roy 1 Jul; Dhyan Chand 29 Aug; Radhakrishnan 5 Sep; Patel 31 Oct; Nehru 14 Nov; Ramanujan 22 Dec; Vajpayee 25 Dec.
2. The exam asks the **person**, not the date — recall who, then check the date.
3. Two teacher-linked days: Teachers' Day (Radhakrishnan) vs Education Day 11 Nov (**Maulana Azad**).

example.q: **National Sports Day** (29 August) commemorates —
example.solution: Major **Dhyan Chand**, the hockey legend — his birth anniversary; the sports awards are conferred on this day.

patterns.name: Day ↔ event commemorated
patterns.howToSpot: 'National Science Day marks', 'Constitution Day is observed because', event-days: Raman effect, Pokhran, Trident, adoption of the Constitution.
patterns.logic:
1. Event-days: Science 28 Feb (**Raman effect, 1928**); Technology 11 May (**Pokhran, 1998**); Navy 4 Dec (**Operation Trident, 1971**); Constitution 26 Nov (**adoption, 1949**); Hindi 14 Sep (**official-language resolution, 1949**).
2. Constitution Day has been observed since **2015** — often asked with its year.
3. Army Day links to **Cariappa (1949)** — a person-event hybrid.

example.q: **National Science Day** (28 February) marks the discovery of —
example.solution: The **Raman effect** (1928) — C.V. Raman's light-scattering work that later won the Nobel Prize.

patterns.name: UN international days and Indian links
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which day did the UN declare on India's proposal', 'World Environment Day is', matching UN days with causes and dates.
patterns.logic:
1. **Yoga — 21 June**: proposed by India, UN-declared **2014**, first observed **2015** — the highest-frequency UN day.
2. Other pins: Environment 5 Jun (Stockholm 1972 origin), Health 7 Apr (WHO, 1948), HR 10 Dec (UDHR, 1948), Non-Violence 2 Oct (Gandhi), UN Day 24 Oct, Press Freedom 3 May.
3. The annual **theme** is the second layer — quote it only within the window.

example.q: The **International Day of Yoga** (21 June) was declared by the UN in —
example.solution: **December 2014**, on **India's proposal** — first observed worldwide on 21 June **2015**.

patterns.name: Defence and service days
patterns.howToSpot: 'Air Force Day is observed on', 'Navy Day commemorates', the three service days and their events.
patterns.logic:
1. Army — **15 January** (Cariappa, 1949); Air Force — **8 October** (its 1932 raising); Navy — **4 December** (Operation Trident, 1971).
2. Ordering hook: January → October → December.
3. Navy Day's Trident was the 1971 missile attack on Karachi harbour — the event asked alongside the date.

example.q: **Indian Air Force Day** is observed on —
example.solution: **8 October** — marking the IAF's raising in 1932; Army Day (15 January) and Navy Day (4 December) complete the trio.

subtopics.title: Indexes and reports — index ↔ publisher
subtopics.concept: The whole game is **index ↔ publisher**: HDI — UNDP; Happiness — UN SDSN; Innovation — WIPO; WEO — IMF; Human Capital — World Bank; Gender Gap/Risks/Tourism — WEF; Corruption — Transparency International; Hunger — Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe (NGOs, not UN); Peace — IEP; Press Freedom — RSF; ASER — Pratham; SDG India and Innovation indexes — NITI Aayog; FI-Index — RBI. Doing Business (World Bank) discontinued 2021 → B-READY 2024.

tricks.title: UN vs NGO split
tricks.body: UN bodies: UNDP (HDI), SDSN (Happiness), WIPO (Innovation), IMF (WEO). NGOs: **Hunger = Concern + Welthungerhilfe**, Peace = IEP, Press = RSF, ASER = Pratham, Corruption = TI.

example.q: Who publishes the Global Hunger Index?
example.solution: Two NGOs — Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe; any UN body in the options is the trap.

mistakes: Attributing the Global Hunger Index to a UN body — it is published by two NGOs.
Crediting the HDI to the World Bank; it belongs to UNDP.
Reciting last year's rank without checking the current edition — ranks, unlike publishers, expire.
subtopics.notes:
### The index ↔ publisher grid — the whole subtopic
Index questions overwhelmingly ask **who releases which index**. Learn the publisher columns; ranks change every edition, publishers never do.

| Index | Publisher | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Human Development Index (HDI)** | **UNDP** (Human Development Report) | Health + education + income; since 1990 |
| World Happiness Report | UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) | March releases |
| Global SDG Index | UN SDSN | Tracks the 17 SDGs |
| **Global Innovation Index** | **WIPO** (Geneva) | Innovation inputs/outputs |
| World Economic Outlook; Global Financial Stability Report | **IMF** | Flagship macro reports |
| Human Capital Index | **World Bank** | Part of the Human Capital Project |
| **Global Gender Gap Report**; Global Risks Report; Travel & Tourism Development Index | **World Economic Forum** (Davos) | WEF's trio |
| **Corruption Perceptions Index** | **Transparency International** (Berlin) | Higher score = cleaner |
| **Global Peace Index** | Institute for Economics & Peace (Sydney) | — |
| **Global Hunger Index** | **Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe** | Two NGOs — not a UN body (classic trap) |
| Henley Passport Index | Henley & Partners | Visa-free access |
| World Competitiveness Index | **IMD** (Lausanne) | — |
| Environmental Performance Index | **Yale + Columbia** universities | Biennial-ish |
| Democracy Index; Global Liveability Index | EIU (Economist Intelligence Unit) | — |
| World Press Freedom Index | **Reporters Without Borders** (RSF) | 3 May links to Press Freedom Day |
| Ease of Doing Business | **DISCONTINUED by the World Bank (2021)** | Replaced by **Business Ready (B-READY)** from 2024 |

### India's own indexes and reports
- **NITI Aayog**: **SDG India Index**, **India Innovation Index** (with Institute for Competitiveness), Composite Water Management Index, Multidimensional Poverty Index (national).
- **RBI**: Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index), and its Handbook of Statistics.
- **MoSPI**: CPI, IIP and the household-consumption surveys (the official statistical base).
- **ASER** (Annual Status of Education Report) — by the NGO **Pratham**, on rural schooling.
- **EF-PII**-style environment reports and the Economic Survey (DEA) round out the domestic set.

### How to answer
1. Match the **publisher first** — three options usually die on a wrong UN family member (e.g. 'Global Hunger Index — UNDP' is false).
2. Know the **UN family vs NGOs** split: UNDP/UNSDSN/WHO/FAO/UNEP/UNICEF are UN bodies; Transparency International, IEP, Concern Worldwide, Pratham, RSF are not.
3. Note **India's rank only within the window** — it changes with each edition; the pairing is permanent.
4. Discontinued and renamed lists matter: Doing Business → **B-READY**; Global Competitiveness paused by WEF.

### Quick revision
- UN bodies: HDI — UNDP; Happiness & SDG — UN SDSN; WEO — IMF; Human Capital — World Bank; Innovation — WIPO.
- WEF trio: Gender Gap, Global Risks, Travel & Tourism. CPI (corruption) — Transparency International, Berlin.
- NGOs: Hunger — Concern + Welthungerhilfe; Peace — IEP; Press Freedom — RSF; ASER — Pratham; EPI — Yale/Columbia; IMD — competitiveness.
- India: SDG India & Innovation indexes — NITI Aayog; FI-Index — RBI; ASER — Pratham.
- Doing Business (World Bank) discontinued 2021 → B-READY.

patterns.name: Index ↔ UN-family publisher
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Human Development Index is released by', 'which body publishes the Global Innovation Index', matching indexes with UN organisations.
patterns.logic:
1. UN-family pins: **HDI — UNDP**; **Happiness — UN SDSN**; **Innovation — WIPO**; WEO — IMF; Human Capital — World Bank.
2. Don't migrate publishers inside the UN family — 'HDI by UNESCO' or 'Innovation by UNDP' are the planted errors.
3. The HDI rides inside the **Human Development Report** — often asked together.

example.q: The **Global Innovation Index** is released by —
example.solution: **WIPO** (World Intellectual Property Organization), Geneva — not UNDP or the WEF.

patterns.name: Index ↔ non-UN publishers (NGOs, think tanks)
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Global Hunger Index is released by', 'the Corruption Perceptions Index comes from', matching NGO/think-tank indexes.
patterns.logic:
1. **Global Hunger Index — Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe** (two NGOs, not UN — the classic trap).
2. **Corruption Perceptions Index — Transparency International** (Berlin); **Global Peace Index — IEP**; **Press Freedom — RSF**; **Democracy/Liveability — EIU**; **EPI — Yale + Columbia**; **Competitiveness — IMD**.
3. WEF's own trio: Gender Gap, Global Risks, Travel & Tourism.

example.q: The **Global Hunger Index** is published by —
example.solution: **Concern Worldwide (Ireland) and Welthungerhilfe (Germany)** — two NGOs; any option naming UNDP/FAO/WHO is wrong.

patterns.name: India-specific indexes and their publishers
patterns.howToSpot: 'The SDG India Index is released by', 'ASER is published by', 'the FI-Index belongs to', matching Indian indexes.
patterns.logic:
1. **NITI Aayog**: SDG India Index, India Innovation Index, Composite Water Index, national MPI.
2. **RBI**: Financial Inclusion (FI) Index; **MoSPI**: CPI/IIP base data.
3. **ASER — Pratham** (NGO) on rural learning levels; Economic Survey — Department of Economic Affairs.

example.q: The **SDG India Index** is released by —
example.solution: **NITI Aayog** — tracking states and UTs on the 17 SDGs; the *global* SDG index, by contrast, comes from the UN SDSN.

patterns.name: Discontinued, renamed and replaced indexes
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Ease of Doing Business index was replaced by', statements noting a discontinued index or a new publisher.
patterns.logic:
1. **Ease of Doing Business — discontinued by the World Bank in 2021**; its successor is **Business Ready (B-READY)**, first edition **2024**.
2. WEF paused its Global Competitiveness Report; older indexes survive in past editions only.
3. When a question cites a discontinued index, the answer usually turns on **who discontinued it and when**.

example.q: The World Bank **discontinued its Ease of Doing Business rankings** in —
example.solution: **2021**, replacing the series with **Business Ready (B-READY)** from 2024 after a data-irregularity review.

solvedExamples.q:
Match the sports award with its field:
1. Khel Ratna 2. Dronacharya 3. MAKA Trophy
(i) coaches (ii) university (iii) highest sporting honour
solvedExamples.solution: Khel Ratna is the **highest sporting honour** (1991-92, renamed 2021), Dronacharya (1985) goes to **coaches**, and the MAKA Trophy (1956-57) to the best **university**. Work the field column first; the years confirm.

solvedExamples.q: **National Sports Day** is observed on 29 August to mark the birth anniversary of —
solvedExamples.solution: **Major Dhyan Chand**, the hockey wizard — 29 August; the sports awards are conferred the same day. Patel rides 31 October, Nehru 14 November and Vivekananda 12 January.

solvedExamples.q: The **Global Hunger Index** is published by —
solvedExamples.solution: Two NGOs — **Concern Worldwide (Ireland) and Welthungerhilfe (Germany)**. Every UN body in the options is the planted trap; the GHI has never been a UN product.

practice.q: A question that gives **two or three numbered statements** and asks which are correct is which frame?
practice.solution: The **statement-based frame** hides one wrong detail (year, ministry, host city) inside mostly true statements — eliminate the planted error and the option set collapses.

practice.q: Pairing **award ↔ field, day ↔ theme, index ↔ publisher** belongs to which frame?
practice.solution: Match-the-column tests **pairs** — the safest method is checking each pair independently; one verified wrong pair eliminates the whole option.

practice.q: In a statement-based CA question, the fastest approach is —
options: Eliminate the option containing a statement with a verified factual error
Read all statements twice, then guess
Choose the option with the most statements
practice.solution: One planted error per set is the norm — a single **verified wrong detail** (wrong year, wrong ministry) knocks out every option containing it.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **standard CA bucket** tracked every month?
practice.solution: Appointments (persons in posts) are one of the **ten fixed buckets** — alongside awards, sports, summits, schemes, defence, space, indexes, days and economy news.

practice.q: Within any news bucket, the items **most frequently asked** are —
practice.solution: Exams love **firsts** (first woman, first Indian), **superlatives** (largest, fastest, highest) and **anniversaries** (X years of an event) — they are precise, checkable and timeless once asked.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Sports winners form a monthly CA bucket.
2. Index ranks and their publishers form a monthly CA bucket.
3. The framing of a pending court case is a common question.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Buckets 1 and 2 are standard. Statement 3 is wrong — **unsettled court arguments and speculation are not asked**; only concluded, factual outcomes appear.

practice.q: The most efficient way to cover a year of current affairs is —
options: One monthly compilation revised multiple times
Reading only the last week's news
practice.solution: **One source, three revisions** (same month, after a month, exam week) — coverage plus retention beats scattered single reads.

practice.q: While noting a **new scheme announcement**, the detail to record for exams is —
practice.solution: Exams ask the **pairing**: which ministry launched it, what it provides, who is eligible. The speech's rhetoric is never the answer.

practice.q: For a **summit** news item, which note is most exam-productive?
options: Host country, theme and membership changes
practice.solution: Summit questions recur on **host, theme, logo, outcomes and new members** — a fixed question shape across years.

practice.q: A news item about a **Nobel Prize** announcement is best revised through —
options: The Nobel prize categories and their structure
practice.solution: The **static root** — six prize categories, Alfred Nobel's will, Peace at Oslo, Economics added in 1969 — serves every year's cycle and often is the tested fact.

practice.q: 'X years of the Constitution' as a news anniversary primarily helps revise —
options: The Constitution's making, parts and Preamble
practice.solution: Anniversaries are bridges to **static topics** — the making of the Constitution, Parts, Schedules and the Preamble — the static layer exams actually test.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about CA preparation:
1. The CA-to-static bridge rewards learning award structures once.
2. Volatile items like a person's current post stay useful only until they change.
3. CA questions never connect to static GK.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — structures endure, offices change. Statement 3 is wrong: the **CA-to-static bridge is one of the four standard frames**.

practice.q: India's **highest civilian award** is —
practice.solution: **Bharat Ratna** (1954) tops the civilian ladder; Param Vir Chakra is a *gallantry* award, not civilian.

practice.q: The **fourth-highest** civilian award of India is —
practice.solution: Order: Bharat Ratna → Padma Vibhushan → Padma Bhushan → **Padma Shri**.

practice.q: The **first woman** to receive the Bharat Ratna was —
practice.solution: **Indira Gandhi (1971)**; Mother Teresa (1980) and Lata Mangeshkar (2001) came later.

practice.q: Padma awards are ordinarily announced on the eve of —
practice.solution: The Padma list is announced on **Republic Day eve** (25 January); gallantry awards also cluster around 26 January and 15 August.

practice.q: The **highest sporting honour** of India is the —
options: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award
practice.solution: The **Khel Ratna** (instituted 1991-92, renamed after Major Dhyan Chand in 2021) is the top sports award.

practice.q: The **Dronacharya Award** is given to outstanding —
practice.solution: **Dronacharya (1985) = coaches** — named after the teacher of archery in the Mahabharata; players get the Arjuna Award.

practice.q: The **MAKA Trophy** is awarded to the best —
practice.solution: The **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (MAKA) Trophy** (1956-57) honours the best **university** in sports.

practice.q:
Arrange by instituting year (earliest first):
1. Arjuna Award 2. Dronacharya Award 3. Khel Ratna
practice.solution: Arjuna **1961** → Dronacharya **1985** → Khel Ratna **1991-92** (renamed Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna, 2021).

practice.q: The **Nobel Peace Prize** is awarded in —
practice.solution: Peace is conferred at **Oslo** (by the Norwegian Nobel Committee); all other categories are presented at **Stockholm**.

practice.q: Which Nobel category was **not** part of Alfred Nobel's original will?
practice.solution: Nobel's 1895 will listed five prizes; **Economics** was added in **1969** as the Sveriges Riksbank memorial prize.

practice.q: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in —
practice.solution: Nobel signed his will in **1895**; the first prizes followed in **1901**.

practice.q: India's **highest wartime gallantry award** is the —
practice.solution: **Param Vir Chakra** (instituted 26 January 1950) is the top wartime gallantry medal; Ashoka Chakra heads the peacetime ladder.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **peacetime** gallantry award?
practice.solution: Peacetime ladder: **Ashoka Chakra > Kirti Chakra > Shaurya Chakra**. The MVC and Vir Chakra are wartime medals.

practice.q: The **Jnanpith Award** is associated with —
practice.solution: The **Jnanpith** is India's highest literary honour — first given in **1965** to **G. Sankara Kurup**.

practice.q: The **Dadasaheb Phalke Award**, first given to Devika Rani, honours —
practice.solution: The highest Indian **cinema** honour — instituted **1969**, first recipient **Devika Rani**.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The first Bharat Ratnas were conferred in 1954.
2. The Ramon Magsaysay Award is presented in Manila.
3. The Bharat Ratna can be awarded posthumously.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are correct — the 1954 first batch, the Manila-based Magsaysay (1957), and posthumous conferral (Shastri, 1966) are settled facts.

practice.q: The **Thomas Cup** is associated with —
practice.solution: The **Thomas Cup** is the men's team badminton world championship; women play for the **Uber Cup**.

practice.q: The **Ranji Trophy** is India's premier —
practice.solution: Started **1934** and named after **Ranjitsinhji**, it is the domestic first-class championship; the IPL (2008) is the T20 league.

practice.q: The **Durand Cup**, Asia's oldest football tournament, began in —
practice.solution: The **Durand Cup (1888)** is Asia's oldest football tournament — a favourite superlative question.

practice.q: The **FIFA World Cup** was first held in —
practice.solution: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in **1930**; the tournament runs every four years.

practice.q: The **ICC T20 World Cup** is held —
practice.solution: The T20 World Cup is **biennial**; the ODI World Cup is four-yearly (first 1975).

practice.q: The **Commonwealth Games** began as the British Empire Games in —
practice.solution: First held at **Hamilton, Canada in 1930** as the British Empire Games; four-yearly thereafter.

practice.q: The **modern Olympic Games** began in —
practice.solution: **1896, Athens** — revived by Pierre de Coubertin; the IOC (1894) is headquartered at **Lausanne**.

practice.q: The Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Communius' adds which idea?
practice.solution: **Communius = 'Together'**, added in 2021 to 'Faster, Higher, Stronger' — the newest static layer of the motto.

practice.q: The first **Winter Olympics** were held at —
practice.solution: **Chamonix, 1924** — the Winter Games run in a separate four-year cycle from the Summer Games.

practice.q: India first participated in the Olympics in —
practice.solution: **1900 Paris** — Norman Pritchard won two athletics silvers; hockey's gold run began only in 1928.

practice.q: How many **Olympic hockey golds** has India won?
practice.solution: **Eight golds** — from Amsterdam 1928 to Moscow 1980, the longest run in Olympic hockey.

practice.q:
Arrange India's sporting firsts chronologically:
1. First Olympic hockey gold 2. First individual Olympic gold 3. First Cricket World Cup win
practice.solution: Hockey gold **1928** → Cricket World Cup **1983** → individual gold (Bindra) **2008**.

practice.q: The **Indian Premier League (IPL)** began in —
practice.solution: The BCCI launched the T20 IPL in **2008** — annual since then.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The first Cricket World Cup was played in 1975.
2. India won the ODI World Cup in 1983 and 2011.
3. The Santosh Trophy is a tennis event.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong — the **Santosh Trophy is football** (inter-state championship).

practice.q: **Khelo India Games** were launched in —
practice.solution: **Khelo India (2018)** — annual school and university games to build a sporting pipeline.

practice.q: The **African Union** joined the G20 as a permanent member at the —
practice.solution: At the **New Delhi G20 (2023)** the AU became the second regional bloc (after the EU) with permanent membership.

practice.q: **QUAD** consists of —
practice.solution: The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue groups **India, the USA, Japan and Australia** — revived in 2017, leaders'-level since 2021.

practice.q: **BRICS expansion**, adding members such as Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE, took effect in —
practice.solution: The bloc expanded from January **2024**; South Africa had joined the original BRIC in 2010, and India-Pakistan entered the SCO in 2017 — don't mix the years.

practice.q: The headquarters of **SAARC** is at —
practice.solution: **Kathmandu** hosts SAARC (founded 1985, first summit at Dhaka); BIMSTEC sits at **Dhaka** — don't swap them.

practice.q: **BIMSTEC** groups how many member states?
practice.solution: **Seven** Bay of Bengal littorals — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand; HQ at **Dhaka**.

practice.q: The **ASEAN** secretariat is located at —
practice.solution: ASEAN (Bangkok Declaration, **1967**) works from **Jakarta**; India is a dialogue partner, not a member.

practice.q: Match: 1. SCO 2. SAARC 3. BIMSTEC — with (i) Kathmandu (ii) Beijing (iii) Dhaka:
practice.solution: SCO → **Beijing**; SAARC → **Kathmandu**; BIMSTEC → **Dhaka** — the three HQs exams swap most often.

practice.q: India is **not** a member of —
practice.solution: **APEC** is the classic trap — India is outside it, though it belongs to BRICS, SCO and BIMSTEC.

practice.q: Regarding **ASEAN**, India is —
options: A sectoral dialogue partner, not a member
practice.solution: India partners ASEAN at summit level but is **not** one of its Southeast Asian members — a fixed distinction in every grouping question.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Commonwealth has 56 member states.
2. India is a member of both SAARC and BIMSTEC.
3. India is a member of the G7.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong — the **G7 excludes India** (US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada).

practice.q: The **Shanghai Cooperation Organisation** was founded in —
practice.solution: The SCO took its present form in **2001** from the earlier Shanghai Five; India and Pakistan joined as full members in 2017.

practice.q: The **first BRICS summit** was held in —
practice.solution: The acronym ('BRIC') was coined in 2001, but the **first summit came in 2009 at Yekaterinburg**; South Africa joined in 2010.

practice.q:
Arrange by founding year (earliest first):
1. ASEAN 2. SAARC 3. G20
practice.solution: ASEAN **1967** → SAARC **1985** → G20 **1999** (leaders' summits from 2008).

practice.q: The **United Nations** currently has —
practice.solution: **193 members** since South Sudan joined in 2011; 51 states founded the UN in 1945.

practice.q: How many times has India been elected a **non-permanent member** of the UNSC?
practice.solution: **Eight terms** — most recently 2021-22; India campaigns for a permanent seat in the reformed Council.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about the UN:
1. It was founded in 1945 with 51 members.
2. The ICJ is its principal judicial organ, seated at The Hague.
3. The UNSC's five permanent members are elected every two years.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong — the **P-5 are permanent** (with veto); only the ten non-permanent seats face election, for two-year terms.

practice.q: **National Youth Day** (12 January) marks the birth anniversary of —
practice.solution: **Swami Vivekananda**, born 12 January 1863 — the day anchors the National Youth Festival.

practice.q: **National Unity Day** (31 October) commemorates —
practice.solution: The **Iron Man's** birth anniversary (31 October 1875) — Rashtriya Ekta Diwas, observed since 2014.

practice.q: **National Education Day** (11 November) honours —
practice.solution: **Maulana Azad**, independent India's first Education Minister, born 11 November 1888 — don't confuse with Teachers' Day (5 September, Radhakrishnan).

practice.q: **National Mathematics Day** (22 December) marks the birth of —
practice.solution: **Ramanujan** (born 22 December 1887); the day has been observed since **2012**, his 125th birth-anniversary year.

practice.q:
Arrange by date within the year:
1. Teachers' Day 2. Children's Day 3. National Sports Day
practice.solution: Sports Day **29 August** → Teachers' Day **5 September** → Children's Day **14 November**.

practice.q: **National Technology Day** (11 May) commemorates —
practice.solution: The **Pokhran-II tests of 11 May 1998**; ISRO-related milestones are marked separately, not on this day.

practice.q: **Constitution Day** (26 November) has been observed since —
practice.solution: The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** and came into force on 26 January 1950; the observance began in **2015** (the 125th birth-anniversary year of Ambedkar).

practice.q: **Navy Day** (4 December) commemorates —
practice.solution: **Operation Trident** — the 1971 missile attack on Karachi harbour; the other operations belong to different services and years.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. National Science Day marks the Raman effect (1928).
2. Army Day is observed on 15 January.
3. Hindi Diwas marks the adoption of Hindi as official language in 1949.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are settled: 28 February (Raman 1928), 15 January (Cariappa 1949), 14 September (1949 resolution).

practice.q: The **International Day of Yoga** (21 June) was first observed in —
practice.solution: The UN declared it in **December 2014** on India's proposal; the first global Yoga Day fell on **21 June 2015**.

practice.q: **World Environment Day** (5 June) traces its origin to —
practice.solution: The UN Conference on the Human Environment at **Stockholm (1972)** both created UNEP and gave the day its start; Rio (1992) came later.

practice.q: **Human Rights Day** (10 December) marks the adoption of —
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
practice.solution: The **UDHR, adopted 10 December 1948** — the UN Charter (1945) and Geneva Conventions are separate instruments.

practice.q: **Indian Air Force Day** is observed on —
practice.solution: **8 October** — the IAF was raised in 1932; 16 December marks Vijay Diwas (1971 victory).

practice.q: Match the service day: 1. Army 2. Air Force 3. Navy — with (i) 8 October (ii) 4 December (iii) 15 January:
practice.solution: Army **15 January** → Air Force **8 October** → Navy **4 December** — chronology makes the trio easy to hold.

practice.q: **Army Day** (15 January) recalls —
options: The raising of the Indian Army
K.M. Cariappa becoming the first Indian Commander-in-Chief
practice.solution: On **15 January 1949** **K.M. Cariappa** took over as the first Indian Commander-in-Chief of the Army.

practice.q: The **Human Development Index (HDI)** is released in the —
practice.solution: The **UNDP's Human Development Report** carries the HDI — health, education and income combined; the WDR belongs to the World Bank and the WEO to the IMF.

practice.q: The **Global Innovation Index** is published by —
practice.solution: **WIPO**, the World Intellectual Property Organization at Geneva, publishes the GII.

practice.q: The **World Happiness Report** is published by —
practice.solution: The **UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network** issues the report each March — not the WHO or the World Bank.

practice.q: Match: 1. HDI 2. World Economic Outlook 3. Global Innovation Index — with (i) IMF (ii) UNDP (iii) WIPO:
practice.solution: HDI → **UNDP**; WEO → **IMF**; GII → **WIPO** — the standard UN-family triple.

practice.q: The **Corruption Perceptions Index** is released by —
practice.solution: **Transparency International (Berlin)** publishes the CPI — higher score means a cleaner public sector.

practice.q: The **Global Peace Index** is released by —
practice.solution: The Sydney-based **IEP**, a think tank — not a UN body; it also issues the Positive Peace report.

practice.q: The **World Press Freedom Index** is compiled by —
practice.solution: **RSF** publishes the annual index each **3 May** — World Press Freedom Day — while UNESCO runs the related prize and day.

practice.q: Which pairing is **wrong**?
options: Environmental Performance Index — Yale and Columbia
practice.solution: The **Global Hunger Index belongs to Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe**, not UNDP — all other pairs are correct.

practice.q: The **SDG India Index** is released by —
practice.solution: **NITI Aayog** tracks states and UTs on the SDGs; MoSPI handles official statistical series instead.

practice.q: The **Annual Status of Education Report (ASER)** is published by —
practice.solution: **Pratham**, an NGO, surveys rural children's reading and arithmetic each year — an outside-the-government report exams quote often.

practice.q: The **Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index)** is released by —
practice.solution: The **RBI's** FI-Index tracks banking, credit and insurance penetration in one number.

practice.q: The World Bank's **Ease of Doing Business** rankings were discontinued in —
practice.solution: Discontinued in **2021** after a data review; the successor series **Business Ready (B-READY)** began in 2024.

practice.q: The successor to the discontinued **Doing Business** rankings is —
practice.solution: **Business Ready (B-READY)**, first released in **2024** by the World Bank, replaced Doing Business.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The WEF publishes the Global Gender Gap Report.
2. The HDI is published by the World Bank.
3. The India Innovation Index is a NITI Aayog product.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong — the **HDI belongs to the UNDP**, not the World Bank.
practice.shortcut: WEF gender gap; UNDP HDI; NITI innovation.
